title: Document rendering and JavaScript indexing
summary: Google processes JavaScript pages in three phases: crawling, rendering and indexing. Pages are queued, and a headless Chromium renders them when resources allow, so check the rendered HTML. Practical consequences from Google's docs: use <a href> links, do not load different content under URL fragments, expect permission prompts to be declined, and note a noindex in the initial HTML may stop rendering, so JavaScript cannot be relied on to remove it.
actions: Check rendered HTML (not just view-source) for the content and links you expect.
Make every navigable link an <a> element with an href.
Do not use URL fragments to load different content.
Do not ship noindex in the initial HTML if JavaScript is meant to remove it.
Give unknown routes a real 404 or noindex instead of a 200 'not found' view.

myths.myth: JavaScript can safely remove a noindex tag after the page loads.
myths.correction: Google says it may skip rendering when it encounters noindex.

myths.myth: Any clickable element is a link to Google.
myths.correction: Google says it uses <a> elements with an href attribute.

items.prompt: Google processes JavaScript web apps in three main phases: crawling, ___ and indexing. Name the middle phase (one word).
items.explanation: Google's JavaScript SEO basics page says it processes JavaScript web apps in three main phases, and lists them as Crawling, Rendering and Indexing.

items.prompt: According to Google, which HTML links can it discover and follow?
options: A. Any element with an onclick handler
B. Text that looks like a URL in a script
C. Buttons that call the History API
D. <a> elements with an href attribute
items.explanation: Correct: Google says it relies on <a> HTML elements with an href attribute. Elements with only onclick handlers, URL-looking text in a script, and buttons calling the History API are not what the page lists; the page names <a> with href.

items.prompt: True or false: Google says a headless Chromium renders the page and executes its JavaScript once Google's resources allow.
items.explanation: Google states: once Google's resources allow, a headless Chromium renders the page and executes the JavaScript.

items.prompt: Why might JavaScript that removes a noindex tag not work as intended? Complete: Google may ___ rendering.
items.explanation: Google says that when it encounters the noindex tag, it may skip rendering, so JavaScript that would remove the tag may never run.

items.prompt: True or false: a page can rely on a notification or location permission prompt to reveal content, because Googlebot will accept it.
items.explanation: Google says to expect Googlebot to decline user permission requests.

items.prompt: Which statement is NOT supported by the saved sources?
options: A. Googlebot queues pages for both crawling and rendering
B. Google renders every page immediately after crawling it
C. Expect Googlebot to decline user permission requests
D. Use tools to check that rendered HTML has the expected content
items.explanation: Correct (unsupported): Google says pages are queued for crawling and rendering and rendered once its resources allow, which contradicts immediate rendering of everything. The other three are in Google's pages: the queue, declining permission requests, and checking rendered HTML with testing tools.

items.prompt: HYPOTHETICAL single-page app: a mistyped URL shows a 'not found' message built by JavaScript but the server returns 200. One of Google's two fixes is to add or change the robots meta tag to which value?
items.explanation: Google's troubleshooting page gives two strategies for this: redirect to a URL where the server responds with a 404, or add or change the robots meta tag to noindex.

items.prompt: A hypothetical developer checklist for a JavaScript site has four items. Which one conflicts with Google's guidance?
options: A. Use <a> elements with href for internal links
B. Redirect unknown routes to a URL that returns 404
C. Load different page content under URL fragments
D. Check that the rendered HTML has the expected content
items.explanation: Correct (the error): Google says not to use fragments to load different page content. The other three follow Google: <a href> links, redirecting to a URL that returns 404, and checking the rendered HTML.

items.prompt: HYPOTHETICAL single-page store. Symptom: the homepage is indexed but deep product pages are not. Evidence: (1) the raw HTML is an empty container; (2) the rendered HTML shows the content; (3) navigation items are <div> elements with click handlers and no href. Best fix?
options: A. Add the rendered JavaScript files to the XML sitemap
B. Block the script folder in robots.txt
C. Add noindex to the homepage
D. Output real <a href> links to product paths
items.explanation: Correct: Google says it follows <a> elements with an href attribute and the rendered content is already visible, so link discovery is the gap. JavaScript files in a sitemap do not create links. noindex on the homepage would hurt the indexed page. Blocking scripts in robots.txt would stop rendering.

items.prompt: HYPOTHETICAL site. Symptom: new landing pages stay out of search. Evidence: (1) the initial HTML ships <meta name="robots" content="noindex">; (2) a script removes the tag after load, intended for production; (3) the production build ships the same HTML template. Best fix?
options: A. Keep the tag and let JavaScript remove it later
B. Add a second script that deletes the tag sooner
C. Ship pages with no noindex in the initial HTML
D. Use a URL fragment so the tag is skipped
items.explanation: Correct: serve production pages without the noindex in the initial HTML. Leaving the tag for JavaScript to remove depends on rendering Google says it may skip. A faster script has the same dependency. A URL fragment is unrelated to robots meta handling.
